fixes.explanation: Yes, ma'am, yes, sir. He says, “in Your word I have put my hope.” Notice what he's doing before dawn: he's up and crying for help. And right there in the same verse, his hope sits in the word.

Hidden isn't the word he uses. He says, “You are near, O LORD, and all Your commandments are true.” The nearness belongs to the LORD, and the commandments are called true. Nothing in the verse calls them hidden.

Correct. He says, “Salvation is far from the wicked because they do not seek Your statutes.” Pay attention to the reason he gives. It's the not seeking. Earlier he says, “in Your word I have put my hope” (Psalm 119:147), so I think he's showing us the other side of that.
Yes. He says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” That's a joy you can picture, someone coming across a big find. The comparison is for his rejoicing in God's promise.

Crops coming in is a happy picture, friend, and I'd be dancing too. But it's not the one in the verse. He says, “I rejoice in Your promise like one who finds great spoil.” Great spoil is the comparison he picks, and a harvest never makes it in.

Yes. Verse 171 says, “My lips pour forth praise, for You teach me Your statutes.” The praise pours out, and God's teaching is the reason he gives. I'd say a lot of us would love a mouth like that on a Monday morning.

Questioned isn't the word in this verse. He says, “May Your hand be ready to help me, for I have chosen Your precepts.” His reason for asking is that he chose them. The verse doesn't say he questioned them.
That's it. Verse 175 says, “Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me.” He wants to live so that he can praise. Praise is the reason he gives for asking to live.

Growing old in peace sounds nice, friend, like a porch and a quiet evening. But he doesn't ask for it here. Verse 175 says, “Let me live to praise You; may Your judgments sustain me.” Praise is the reason he gives.
